newsitem.title: GERMANY: MILD MARCH WEATHER PUSHES GERMAN UNEMPLOYMENT DOWN.
newsitem.headline: MILD MARCH WEATHER PUSHES GERMAN UNEMPLOYMENT DOWN.

text.p: German unemployment fell slightly in March from the alarming level of the month before, raising some hopes that a turnaround in the jobs market might be starting, the Federal Labour Office said on Tuesday.
Seasonally adjusted unemployment fell by 15,000 to 4.3 million. February data were also revised to show the first fall in the underlying unemployment trend since April 1996.
But the fall was mainly due to milder weather, which allowed construction labourers to return to work, while the trend in manufacturing and other sectors remained weak.
Continuing high unemployment means the government still faces a challenge in reining in the budget deficit to qualify for European monetary union (EMU), analysts said.
The labour data also dim the outlook for any further German interest rate cuts, they added.
Data from the Bundesbank put seasonally-adjusted unemployment at 11.2 percent of the workforce in March, down from 11.3 percent in February.
"The recovery will not be strong enough to lower the unemployment rate significantly," said analyst Julian Kapfhammer at Hypo/VW Research.
Some analysts took an even more negative view. "The turnaround is not yet here," said Trinkaus Capital Management in a research note.

"Unemployment will show further small improvements in coming months in the traditional spring recovery. But in summer unemployment will rise again due to terminations at the end of the quarter and ahead of school vacations," Trinkaus said.

Unadjusted unemployment -- the most politically sensitive jobs figure in Germany -- fell to 4.48 million from February's 4.67 million, which was the highest since 1933. Unadjusted unemployment was still around 340,000 up March 1996.

Unemployment affects Germany's ability to cut its budget deficit as unemployment eats into tax revenue while boosting spending for benefits. Germany, like other European nations, aims to cut its deficit to three percent of economic output this year to qualify for EMU.
"By no means do one month's labour market data change the outlook for Germany's chances of qualifying for EMU in a significant way," said Holger Fahrinkrug at UBS.

"Our budget deficit forecast of 3.4 percent is based on the assumption that unemployment will fall slightly toward the end of 1997 and in 1998, but should remain above the government's forecast," Fahrinkrug said.

The jobless data were not strong enough to prompt worries about wage and inflation pressures, as Germany lagged the United States and Britain in the economic cycle, he added. "But the potential for lower interest rates should be very limited."

Labour Office President Bernhard Jagoda said it was still possible for Germany to post average unadjusted unemployment of 4.2 million for 1997, the figure that underlies government forecasts of meeting the three percent deficit target.
He again urged German employers to fight unemployment by hiring more trainees. He also said there was potential for the services and export sectors to boost job creation.
"Job creation can't be based on individual sectors alone, but I would like to see the service sector growing and I think we could see impetus from export industries," he said.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), who have slid behind the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) in opinion polls largely as a result of the dramatic rise in unemployment, said the figures gave cause for optimism.

"The new unemployment data show that we can achieve a turnaround on the labour market in 1997," CDU general secretary Peter Hintze said in a statement, urging the SPD to cooperate with the government in pushing through planned tax cuts.
"We must implement the tax reform fast. Every moment we delay is a blow to the unemployed," he said.
But the continued high level of unemployment underscores the difficulty of turning to spending cuts as a way to reduce the deficit.

"Experience with many austerity packages in the past shows clearly that these misguided measures have not brought the unemployment problem or public finances under control," said Ursula Konitzer of the DAG white-collar union.
